label: Retirement
framing: The work that defined your days ends, and the question underneath the gold watch is what your life is for now. Scripture has no category for a retreat into mere leisure, but it does offer something better, a final season aimed not at the self but at finishing well and handing on what you have gathered.
cultural: Our culture sells retirement as a long reward, a permanent vacation that quietly tells the old they are now spectators. The Bible never sidelines its elders. It seats them at the center as the keepers of memory and counsel, and it measures a life not by how comfortably it ends but by whether it bears fruit even in old age.
historical: Caleb, near 1400 BC, stood at eighty-five and asked for a mountain still to be conquered, refusing to coast on past faithfulness. Across history the church has given its later years to prayer, mentoring, and works of mercy, from the widows of the early church devoted to intercession to the countless aging saints who found their deepest usefulness only after the paycheck stopped.
application: Resist the drift into a life that orbits only your own comfort, which dulls the soul faster than any disease. Ask what God has freed you to do now that the career no longer claims your hours, then give yourself to it. Invest in the young, the church, and the neighbor, and treat your accumulated wisdom as a deposit meant to be spent. The last third of life can be its most fruitful if it is aimed outward.

verses.text: But at the age of fifty, they must retire from performing the work and no longer serve. After that, they may assist their brothers in fulfilling their duties at the Tent of Meeting, but they themselves are not to do the work. This is how you are to assign responsibilities to the Levites.”
verses.where: At fifty the Levites stop the heavy work of the Tent of Meeting, and after that they may assist their brothers in their duties. The site's note on the chapter says older Levites could assist but not carry the heavy work, and asks what that pattern teaches about changing roles in service as we age. The law knew of a retirement, and it was a change of work, not an end of it.

verses.text: Now behold, as the LORD promised, He has kept me alive these forty-five years since He spoke this word to Moses, while Israel wandered in the wilderness. So here I am today, eighty-five years old, still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me out. As my strength was then, so it is now for war, for going out, and for coming in. Now therefore give me this hill country that the LORD promised me on that day, for you yourself heard then that the Anakim were there, with great and fortified cities. Perhaps with the LORD’s help I will drive them out, as the LORD has spoken.”
verses.where: At eighty-five Caleb reminds Joshua of a promise made forty-five years before and asks for the hill country still held by the Anakim. The site's note on the chapter asks what it would look like to seek a hard task rather than a comfortable retirement from faithfulness. Caleb's strength in the verse is his own testimony, and his request rests on the LORD's help.

verses.text: There was also a prophetess named Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, who was well along in years. She had been married for seven years, and then was a widow to the age of eighty-four. She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying. Coming forward at that moment, she gave thanks to God and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
verses.where: Anna, widowed young and now eighty-four, never leaves the temple, worships night and day, and is the one who speaks about the child to all who are waiting. The site's plain note says she shows that a life many would call empty, old, widowed and alone, can be full before God, and that her years of waiting made her ready to see. It says to anyone who feels their best years are past that God has not finished with them.

verses.text: But Barzillai replied, “How many years of my life remain, that I should go up to Jerusalem with the king? I am now eighty years old. Can I discern what is good and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I still hear the voice of singing men and women? Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?
verses.where: Barzillai, who had provided for David at Mahanaim, is invited to the court at eighty and declines, asking why he should be a burden to the king, and sends a younger man, Chimham, in his place. The site's note on the chapter asks what his contentment to go home and let a younger man receive the reward teaches about aging and generosity. Stepping aside can be a gift as well as a loss.

verses.text: Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good.
verses.where: Paul tells Titus that older men are to be sound in faith, love and perseverance, and older women are to be teachers of good. The site's plain note says Paul gives older women real teaching work and asks older believers to teach younger ones by word and by life. It asks whom you could encourage or teach.

verses.text: Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray. I have made you, and I will carry you; I will sustain you and deliver you.
verses.where: God says he will carry his people even to old age and gray hair: I have made you, and I will carry you. The site's note on the chapter sets this against the gods of Babylon, heavy statues that had to be loaded onto weary animals and hauled away. The God of Israel does not need carrying; he carries.

verses.text: Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is attained along the path of righteousness.
verses.where: Gray hair is a crown of glory, attained along the path of righteousness. The site's note on the chapter lists it among the book's famous sayings. Age in Proverbs is not something to hide but a sign of a long road walked.

verses.text: Then King Rehoboam consulted with the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime. “How do you advise me to respond to these people?” he asked. They replied, “If you will be a servant to these people and serve them this day, and if you will respond by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” But Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders; instead, he consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him.
verses.where: Rehoboam asks the elders who served his father, and they tell him to serve the people and speak kindly, but he rejects their counsel for the young men he grew up with. The site's note on the chapter says the kingdom divided as a result, and asks whose counsel you tend to seek and why. The elders' experience was the one thing the young king most needed and least wanted.

verses.text: Then Joseph brought in his father Jacob and presented him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh. “How many years have you lived?” Pharaoh asked. “My travels have lasted 130 years,” Jacob replied. “My years have been few and hard, and they have not matched the years of the travels of my fathers.” Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh and departed from his presence.
verses.where: Brought before Pharaoh, the aged Jacob calls his years few and hard, and still blesses the most powerful man in the world, twice. The site's note says faith does not require calling a hard life easy, and the plain note says the man who said few and hard still had a blessing to give. An old life with regrets in it is not a life with nothing to offer.

verses.text: He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.” And Naomi took the child, placed him on her lap, and became a nurse to him.
verses.where: The women of Bethlehem tell Naomi that her grandson will renew her life and sustain her in her old age, and she takes the child on her lap and becomes his nurse. The site's note on the chapter says the book closes by turning this family story into part of Israel's history, and asks how ordinary faithfulness may belong to a larger story you cannot yet see. Naomi had called herself bitter when she came home.

links.label: Practical guides for work and money

misread.taken: The rich fool who tells himself to take it easy, eat, drink and be merry is read as a condemnation of saving for retirement or planning for old age, or else waved away as having nothing to do with the plans people actually make.
misread.says: The site's plain note says the story is not against saving or planning, since Scripture praises Joseph and the ant for storing up; the man's sin was greed, storing up treasure for himself while not being rich toward God, and a plan for a life with no one else in it. The note on verse 21 says the verse does not condemn saving as such but a life whose treasure has only one beneficiary. The plain note asks what being rich toward God would look like with what you have.
misread.text: Then I will say to myself, “You have plenty of good things laid up for many years. Take it easy. Eat, drink, and be merry!”’ But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?’

whole: Retirement arrives differently for everyone. For some it is a long-awaited freedom, for others a shock: a farewell lunch, a last badge handed in, and then a Monday with nowhere to be. Some miss the people more than the work. Some discover how much of their sense of who they were came from a title, a desk or being needed. Many face it alongside other changes, a body that is slower, money that must be stretched, a spouse suddenly at home all day, friends beginning to die. And many feel the culture's quiet message that the old are now spectators, and wonder whether they still matter.

Scripture does not see old age that way. The law let Levites step back from the heavy work at fifty, but they went on assisting their brothers. Caleb asked for a hard task at eighty-five. Anna, widowed and old, was the one who recognized the child in the temple and spoke of him to everyone waiting. The trouble is not that work ends, which is often right, but what takes its place. Jesus' parable of the rich man who told himself to take it easy names one danger: a plan for the later years with no one else in it. The other danger is the despair of the person who believes their usefulness ended with their job.

So the Bible's wisdom points outward. Paul asks older men and women to teach the young by word and by life, and the elders' counsel to Rehoboam shows what is lost when the young will not listen. Barzillai stepped aside and sent a younger man in his place, which is its own generosity. Naomi, who had called herself bitter, took her grandson on her lap. In practice this may mean mentoring, serving in the church, caring for grandchildren or neighbours, praying for others by name, or taking on some hard and unpaid task that was impossible while the job filled the week. It also means rest without guilt, and honest planning for money and health with people qualified to help. Where the change has brought you low, tell someone; the site's note on Psalm 71 says you do not have to carry it alone.

The hope Scripture gives is that God does not retire from his people. He says he will carry them to old age and gray hair, and gray hair is a crown in Proverbs, not something to hide. Jacob called his years few and hard and still blessed a king. The psalmist asks not to be forsaken when old and gray until he has told the next generation of God's power. That prayer is answered every time an older believer tells a younger one what God has done.
deep.sit: Who younger than you needs to hear what God has done in your life, and when could you tell them?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says that if you are old this psalm is your prayer, that you are allowed to be afraid of weakness and of being set aside, and that verse 18 means you still have work to do: someone younger needs to hear what God has done in your long life.
prayer.text: O God, You have taught me from my youth, and to this day I proclaim Your marvelous deeds. Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation, Your might to all who are to come.

careLines.text: If the weakness of age has brought you low in spirit, you do not have to carry that alone.
Tell someone you trust, a family member, a pastor or a doctor.
